cases.en_html:
1) [Se'if 1] Since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. Kindling likewise, since it was permitted for food preparation, was also permitted for a non-food need, as stated above at the beginning of siman 511. The same applies to the other labors involved in food preparation, such as slaughtering, baking, and cooking. If one performs them for no need at all or for a weekday, some say that he nevertheless does not incur lashes. Others say that they were permitted for a non-food purpose only when there is some need for that day, such as carrying a child or lulav, or a mitzvah need. When there is neither a mitzvah need nor any ordinary need that day, as when carrying stones, he incurs lashes, as Maggid Mishneh writes in chapter 1, halachah 1. See also below, paragraph 12, and the beginning of siman 527.
2) There: Since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. This applies even when carrying through a public domain, as explained in the Mishnah, Beitzah 12a. The Rosh there, Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34, and the other later authorities write likewise.
3) There: Such as a child, etc. Rabbeinu Chananel explains: a child to be circumcised, a lulav with which to fulfill the mitzvah, and a Torah scroll from which to read. Tosafos there writes that the child need not specifically be carried for circumcision; carrying him for an outing is likewise permitted. The Rosh writes that if one needs to go to the synagogue or take a Yom Tov pleasure walk and cannot leave the child alone at home, he may carry the child with him. Tur and Levush write likewise. Ran, however, explains it as a child carried either for circumcision or for an outing, because that entails Yom Tov enjoyment. Yam Shel Shlomo there similarly writes that the "child" mentioned may be carried even merely for an outing. Magen Avraham, paragraph 1; Chemed Moshe, paragraph 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 3; Mikra'ei Kodesh, siman 12, paragraph 1; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 3.
4) There: Such as a child and a lulav, etc. This implies that carrying for another mitzvah that is not needed that day is forbidden. Bach; Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos on the Tur, paragraph 1; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 1; Mishbetzos Zahav, paragraph 1.
5) There: And a Torah scroll. The same applies to bringing books along to the synagogue and even returning them, for the Sages permitted the return so that people would bring them initially. The Rosh there, cited by Beis Yosef; Olas Shabbos, paragraph 1; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 2; Chemed Moshe there; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there; Mikra'ei Kodesh there. This means that if one fears they will be stolen, he may return them; if there is no concern of theft, returning them is forbidden. Even when theft is a concern, if they had already been left there for many days, returning them is forbidden. Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34; Olas Shabbos there; Magen Avraham, paragraph 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 1; Mikra'ei Kodesh there. This applies when one does not intend to study from them again that day. Olas Shabbos there. If he wishes to recite songs and praises from machzorim on Yom Tov, however, he may always bring them. Chayei Adam and Mikra'ei Kodesh there. The same applies to other books: if he wishes to study them, he may carry them in every circumstance. This follows from the poskim, and Mishbetzos Zahav, paragraph 1, explicitly writes that books from which to study a fixed lesson are a need of that day.
5) Any carrying permitted for a Yom Tov need because it parallels food preparation is likewise permitted for jewelry because of the honor of Yom Tov. The Rosh, first chapter of Beitzah, citing a responsum of the Geonim; Tur; Levush; Taz, paragraph 1; Olas Shabbos there; Chayei Adam there; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 5. See above, siman 516, paragraph 21, and siman 303, paragraph 112.
6) There: And utensils. Gloss: That he needs somewhat. This implies that according to Shulchan Aruch it is permitted even if he has no need for them at all. Although Beis Yosef appears uncertain whether some need is required, Shulchan Aruch here rules without qualification to permit, in accordance with the implication of Rif and Rambam cited in Beis Yosef. Vilna Gaon likewise explains that Rif, Rambam, and Shulchan Aruch permit even when there is no need at all, following the plain Gemara: since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. Maamar Mordechai, paragraph 1, writes similarly, though he subsequently says that Shulchan Aruch remained uncertain, as in Beis Yosef, and therefore decided neither to prohibit nor permit but left his wording unqualified. Shulchan Gavoah, paragraph 2, writes that Rema's gloss explains Shulchan Aruch rather than disagrees with it. Yad Aharon, Hagahos Beis Yosef, writes likewise. Shulchan Aruch's words can thus be understood either way. Rema in his gloss definitively prohibits carrying unless there is some need, etc. Levush; Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34; Taz, paragraph 1; Chemed Moshe, paragraph 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 1; Mikra'ei Kodesh, siman 12, paragraph 1; Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Bamidbar, paragraph 9; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 5, rule likewise.
7) There: And utensils. On Yom Tov one may transport utensils within the techum from a city to a village for a mitzvah meal when the host did not prepare all the necessary utensils. Responsa Chasam Sofer, siman 147; Pischei Teshuvah.
8) There, gloss: That he needs somewhat. Regarding carrying knives, Yam Shel Shlomo writes: In my youth I saw people careful not to carry knives when going for a walk outside the city on Yom Tov, because after the meal the knives were no longer needed that day. Within the city but outside the eruv, however, they would carry them. Taz, paragraph 2, disagrees, writing that knives are certainly considered necessary for food throughout the day, because if one encounters a fruit he can eat it with them. Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 5, agrees, as does Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1. Magen Avraham, paragraph 2, however, cites Yam Shel Shlomo without disagreement, implying that he accepts his view. Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 2, likewise rules so. Nevertheless, even according to Taz, if one knows with certainty that he will not need a knife on this outing (for example, when going to the synagogue or the like) it is forbidden to carry it. Shulchan Aruch HaRav there and Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 10, write likewise.
9) A timepiece, however, may be carried according to all opinions, because it is needed at all times. These laws apply to women as well as men. Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Bamidbar, paragraph 9.

או' ה' ועיין לעיל סי' תקט"ז או' כ"א וסי' ש"ג או קי"ב: ו) שם. וכלים. הגה, הצריכים לו קצת. משמע אבל לדעת הש"ע אעפ"י שא"צ לו כלל שרי והגם שבב"י משמע דמספקא ליה או בעינן צריכין לו קצת הכא סתם להתיר כמשמעות דברי הרי"ף והרמב"ם שהביא בב"י יעו"ש. וכ"כ בביאורי הגר"א דדעת הרי"ף והרמב"ם והש"ע דאף שלא לצורך כלל מותר כפשטא דגמ' מתוך שהותרה הוצאה לצורך וכו' יעו"ש. וכ"כ המאמ"ר או' א' אלא שאח"כ כתב דהש"ע ספוקי מספקא ליה כמ"ש בב"י וע"כ לא החליט הדבר בש"ע לא לאיסור ולא להיתר וסתם דבריו יעו"ש. והשו"ג או' ב' כתב על דברי הגה הנז' דפרושי קא מפרש דברי הש"ע יעו"ש. וכ"כ י"א בהגב"י. נמצא בדברי הש"ע איכא למימר הכי ואיכא למימר הכי ומור"ם ז"ל בהג"ה החליט לאסור אם לא לצורך קצת וכו' וכן פסק הלבוש. יש"ש פ"ק דביצה סי' ל"ד. ט"ז סק"א. חמ"מ או' א' ר"ז או' א' ח"א כלל צ"ו או' א' מק"ק סי' י"ב או' א' בן א"ח פ' במדבר או' ט' מ"ב או' ה': ז) שם. וכלים. ומותר להוליך כלים ביו"ט מעיר לכפר לתוך התחום לצורך סעודת מצוה שלא הכין לו כלים כל צרכו. תשו' חת"ס סי' קמ"ז. פ"ת: ח) שם הגה. הצריכים לו קצת. ולענין הוצאת סכינים כתב שם היש"ש בימי חרפי ראיתי שנזהרים כשהולכים לטייל חוץ לעיר ביו"ט שלא היו נושאים הסכינים עמהם מטעם שהסכינים אחר אכילה אין בהם צורך היום אבל בתוך העיר חוץ לעירוב היו נושאין יעו"ש. אבל הט"ז סק"ב חלק עליו דכתב דודאי סכינים כל היום מקרי צורך אוכל נפש דאי מזדמן ליה איזה פרי יאכל בהם יעו"ש. וכן הסכים א"ר או' ה' וכ"פ הר"ז או' א' מיהו המ"א סק"ב הביא דברי היש"ש הנ"ז ולא חלק עליו ומשמע שמסכים לדבריו. וכ"כ ח"א כלל צ"ו או' ב' ומ"מ גם לדברי הט"ז אם ידוע לו בודאי שלא יצטרך לסכין בהליכה זו כגון שהולך לבהכ"נ וכה"ג אסור להוליכו עמו. וכ"כ הר"ז שם. מ"ב או' יו"ד: ט) אבל כלי המורה שעות מותר לשאת אותו לכ"ע שזה יש בו צורך בכל עת. ודברים אלו שייכים גם בנשים כמו באנשים. בן א"ח פ' במדבר או' ט':
cases.en_plain: 1) [Se'if 1] Since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. Kindling likewise, since it was permitted for food preparation, was also permitted for a non-food need, as stated above at the beginning of siman 511. The same applies to the other labors involved in food preparation, such as slaughtering, baking, and cooking. If one performs them for no need at all or for a weekday, some say that he nevertheless does not incur lashes. Others say that they were permitted for a non-food purpose only when there is some need for that day, such as carrying a child or lulav, or a mitzvah need. When there is neither a mitzvah need nor any ordinary need that day, as when carrying stones, he incurs lashes, as Maggid Mishneh writes in chapter 1, halachah 1. See also below, paragraph 12, and the beginning of siman 527. 2) There: Since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. This applies even when carrying through a public domain, as explained in the Mishnah, Beitzah 12a. The Rosh there, Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34, and the other later authorities write likewise. 3) There: Such as a child, etc. Rabbeinu Chananel explains: a child to be circumcised, a lulav with which to fulfill the mitzvah, and a Torah scroll from which to read. Tosafos there writes that the child need not specifically be carried for circumcision; carrying him for an outing is likewise permitted. The Rosh writes that if one needs to go to the synagogue or take a Yom Tov pleasure walk and cannot leave the child alone at home, he may carry the child with him. Tur and Levush write likewise. Ran, however, explains it as a child carried either for circumcision or for an outing, because that entails Yom Tov enjoyment. Yam Shel Shlomo there similarly writes that the "child" mentioned may be carried even merely for an outing. Magen Avraham, paragraph 1; Chemed Moshe, paragraph 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 3; Mikra'ei Kodesh, siman 12, paragraph 1; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 3. 4) There: Such as a child and a lulav, etc. This implies that carrying for another mitzvah that is not needed that day is forbidden. Bach; Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos on the Tur, paragraph 1; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 1; Mishbetzos Zahav, paragraph 1. 5) There: And a Torah scroll. The same applies to bringing books along to the synagogue and even returning them, for the Sages permitted the return so that people would bring them initially. The Rosh there, cited by Beis Yosef; Olas Shabbos, paragraph 1; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 2; Chemed Moshe there; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there; Mikra'ei Kodesh there. This means that if one fears they will be stolen, he may return them; if there is no concern of theft, returning them is forbidden. Even when theft is a concern, if they had already been left there for many days, returning them is forbidden. Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34; Olas Shabbos there; Magen Avraham, paragraph 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 1; Mikra'ei Kodesh there. This applies when one does not intend to study from them again that day. Olas Shabbos there. If he wishes to recite songs and praises from machzorim on Yom Tov, however, he may always bring them. Chayei Adam and Mikra'ei Kodesh there. The same applies to other books: if he wishes to study them, he may carry them in every circumstance. This follows from the poskim, and Mishbetzos Zahav, paragraph 1, explicitly writes that books from which to study a fixed lesson are a need of that day. 5) Any carrying permitted for a Yom Tov need because it parallels food preparation is likewise permitted for jewelry because of the honor of Yom Tov. The Rosh, first chapter of Beitzah, citing a responsum of the Geonim; Tur; Levush; Taz, paragraph 1; Olas Shabbos there; Chayei Adam there; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 5. See above, siman 516, paragraph 21, and siman 303, paragraph 112. 6) There: And utensils. Gloss: That he needs somewhat. This implies that according to Shulchan Aruch it is permitted even if he has no need for them at all. Although Beis Yosef appears uncertain whether some need is required, Shulchan Aruch here rules without qualification to permit, in accordance with the implication of Rif and Rambam cited in Beis Yosef. Vilna Gaon likewise explains that Rif, Rambam, and Shulchan Aruch permit even when there is no need at all, following the plain Gemara: since carrying was permitted for a need, etc. Maamar Mordechai, paragraph 1, writes similarly, though he subsequently says that Shulchan Aruch remained uncertain, as in Beis Yosef, and therefore decided neither to prohibit nor permit but left his wording unqualified. Shulchan Gavoah, paragraph 2, writes that Rema's gloss explains Shulchan Aruch rather than disagrees with it. Yad Aharon, Hagahos Beis Yosef, writes likewise. Shulchan Aruch's words can thus be understood either way. Rema in his gloss definitively prohibits carrying unless there is some need, etc. Levush; Yam Shel Shlomo, first chapter of Beitzah, siman 34; Taz, paragraph 1; Chemed Moshe, paragraph 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1; Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 1; Mikra'ei Kodesh, siman 12, paragraph 1; Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Bamidbar, paragraph 9; Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 5, rule likewise. 7) There: And utensils. On Yom Tov one may transport utensils within the techum from a city to a village for a mitzvah meal when the host did not prepare all the necessary utensils. Responsa Chasam Sofer, siman 147; Pischei Teshuvah. 8) There, gloss: That he needs somewhat. Regarding carrying knives, Yam Shel Shlomo writes: In my youth I saw people careful not to carry knives when going for a walk outside the city on Yom Tov, because after the meal the knives were no longer needed that day. Within the city but outside the eruv, however, they would carry them. Taz, paragraph 2, disagrees, writing that knives are certainly considered necessary for food throughout the day, because if one encounters a fruit he can eat it with them. Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 5, agrees, as does Shulchan Aruch HaRav, paragraph 1. Magen Avraham, paragraph 2, however, cites Yam Shel Shlomo without disagreement, implying that he accepts his view. Chayei Adam, rule 96, paragraph 2, likewise rules so. Nevertheless, even according to Taz, if one knows with certainty that he will not need a knife on this outing (for example, when going to the synagogue or the like) it is forbidden to carry it. Shulchan Aruch HaRav there and Mishnah Berurah, paragraph 10, write likewise. 9) A timepiece, however, may be carried according to all opinions, because it is needed at all times. These laws apply to women as well as men. Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Bamidbar, paragraph 9.

בי"ט שני כו'. ובכ"ה משמע דבמדינות תוגרמה שדרין שם יהודים רבים אין להתיר לקוברו בי"ט שני ע"י ישראל אלא באדם מפורסם כמ"ש רי"ו ואף על גב שנתפרסם הדבר בעיר לא מהני והליכה חוץ לתחום דמי לקציצת ארזים דאסור אף באדם מפורסם (ת"י קי"ד):
כחול וכו'. אבל י"ט שני של ימים הראשונים הוה כח"ה (ת"י ת"ד) והתו' כתבו דאין לחלק (כ"ה):
כמו בי"ט ראשון. וביש"ש כ' דמותר לטהרו בסדין בי"ט שני כיון דאינו אלא גזיר' שמא יסחוט רק שיזהרו שלא יעשו סחיטה בידים:
לכסותו בעפר. דגמר קבורה היא (ב"י) ולכאור' למנהג שלנו הוא אסור דהא כתב ת"ה שאנו נוהגין שלא לעשות מלאכה דאוריית' והרב"י כ' דסתימת הקבר הוי מלאכה דאוריית' ובס' ראב"ן כ' גבי יום טוב ראשון שיכסוהו עכו"ם ובט"ז בי"ד כ' ראיתי קצת מקומות שישראלים מחזירים העפר לתוך הקבר והוא בעיני איסור גמור וכו' ע"ש ובלבוש כ' בי"ט שני יש אוסרין ויש מתירין ויש להקל עכ"ל אפש' דס"ל דלא הוי מלאכה דאורייתא דאמרי' בשבת דף פ"א אסו' לפנות בשדה ניר בשבת (פירש"י ור"ן בחרישה ראשונה ועומדת לזריעה) דלמ' שקיל צרור מעילאי ושדי ליה לתתאי והסותם גומא בשדה חייב משום חורש בבית חייב משום בונה ע"כ משמע דבשדה שאינו חרושה לא מחייב כלל מיהו אפשר דזה דמי לבית שמתקן בזה שלא יהא המת מגולה ולכן נ"ל דאסו' ובס' מ"ש החמיר מאד וכ' מקום שנהגו לקבור על ידי ישראל לא יחפרו אנשים אחרים זולת בני החבורה הרגילין לחפור וכ"ש שלא ישליכו אנשים אחרים עפר לסתום הקבר דכל מה דאפשר למעט בחלול ממעטי' עכ"ל ורש"מ סי' י"ו מתיר לכל ע"ש וכנ"ל דהא כחול שווי' רבנן וגדולה מזו אמרו גבי מילה בשבת דמותרים שני מוהלים למול כמ"ש בי"ד עסי' רס"ו ק"ו כאן:
אבל טלטול מותר. אבל אסו' להוציאו אפי' לכרמלי' ואף על גב דמשמע ברש"י ורא"ש דמות' לכבסו ולגזוז שערו מ"מ הוצא' היא מלאכ' טפי דגזיזת שער במת אינו מלאכה כלל (ת"ה) וביש"ש הקשה דהא כ' הרמב"ם פ"ט הגוזז בין מן החי בין מן במת חייב וכ"ה בירושלמי פ' כלל גדול אלא ע"כ דעת הרא"ש לפירש"י דמלאכה כבידה אסור אבל הוצאה שרי ומ"מ נ"ל שט"ס הוא ברש"י וצריך להגיה א"כ כו' ע"ש וא"כ אסור לעשות שום דבר לצורך מחר עכ"ל עס"ח ול"נ דמ"ש בת"ה דגזיזות שער אינה מלאכה כלל היינו משום שא"צ לשער כלל והרמב"ם מיירי בצריך לשער עמ"ש סי' ש"מ ואף על גב דהוצאה נמי הוה מלאכ' שא"צ לגופו מ"מ שם הוצאה עליה אבל הכא לא הוי מלאכה כלל דהא אמרי' בשבת אם מל תינוק בן ח' בשבת לא עביד כלום דהוי מחתך בשר בעלמ' כ"ש שער ומ"מ טוב להחמיר וכ"מ בת"ה ובש"ע:

On the second day of Yom Tov, etc. In Kenesses HaGedolah it implies that in the lands of Togarmah, where many Jews live, one should not permit burying him on the second day of Yom Tov through Jews except for a distinguished person, as Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote. Even if the matter became known in the city, that does not help. Going outside the techum is comparable to cutting cedars, which is forbidden even for a distinguished person, as in Tashbetz, siman 114.
Like a weekday, etc. But the second day of Yom Tov of the first days is like Chol HaMoed, as in Tashbetz, siman 404; Tosafot wrote that one should not distinguish, and so it is.
As on the first day of Yom Tov. In Yam Shel Shlomo he wrote that it is permitted to purify him with a sheet on the second day of Yom Tov, since it is only a decree lest one squeeze; one must only be careful not to squeeze actively.
To cover it with earth. For this is the completion of burial, as in the Beis Yosef. At first glance, according to our practice this is forbidden, for Terumas HaDeshen wrote that our practice is not to perform labor according to the Torah, and the Beis Yosef wrote that closing the grave is labor according to the Torah. In Sefer Raavan he wrote regarding the first day of Yom Tov that non-Jews should cover him. In the Taz in Yoreh Deah he wrote: I saw some places where Jews return the earth into the grave, and in my eyes this is a complete prohibition, etc.; see there. In Levush he wrote that on the second day of Yom Tov some forbid and some permit, and one may be lenient, end quote. Perhaps he holds that it is not labor according to the Torah, for we say in Shabbos, folio 81, that one may not relieve himself in a plowed field on Shabbos, for perhaps he will take a clod from above and throw it below; one who fills a hole in a field is liable because of plowing, and in a house because of building. This implies that in a field that is not plowed he is not liable at all. However, perhaps this is comparable to a house, since he repairs it thereby so that the dead will not be exposed. Therefore it seems to me that it is forbidden. In Sefer Masas Binyamin he was very stringent and wrote that in a place where the custom is to bury through Jews, no other men should dig except the members of the society accustomed to digging, and all the more so other people should not throw earth to close the grave, for whatever can be minimized in desecration, we minimize, end quote. Responsa of Shlomo ben Shimon Duran, siman 16, permits everyone; see there. This appears correct to me, for the Sages treated it like a weekday, and they said something even greater regarding circumcision on Shabbos, that two mohalim may circumcise, as written in Yoreh Deah; see siman 266. All the more so here.
But moving is permitted. But it is forbidden to take him out even to a karmelis. Although it implies from Rashi and the Rosh that it is permitted to wash him and cut his hair, nevertheless carrying out is more of a labor, for cutting hair on a corpse is not a labor at all, as in Terumas HaDeshen. In Yam Shel Shlomo he objected: the Rambam wrote in chapter 9 that one who shears, whether from a living being or from a corpse, is liable, and so it is in the Yerushalmi, chapter Klal Gadol. Rather, the view of the Rosh according to Rashi must be that a weighty labor is forbidden but carrying is permitted. Nevertheless, it seems to me that there is a textual error in Rashi and one must emend it; see there. Accordingly, it is forbidden to do anything for the need of tomorrow, end quote; see seif 8. {מח} נפלים וכו' - נראה דלאו בנפלים ודאים קאמר דהא אינהו אסור לקוברם ביו"ט וא"כ בלאו הכי לא שייך למוהלן דהא מלין אותן על קברן וכמו שכתב המחבר ביו"ד בסימן רס"ג סעיף ה' אלא אנפלים דסעיף ט' קאי שמחזקינן להו לענין קבורה בחזקת בני קיימא ומטפלין בקבורתם ביום טוב ואפילו הכי לקיים המנהג למולן אין להתיר שאין זה מצרכי קבורה:
{מט} ואסור לקוברו - לפי מה שבארנו דברי המחבר אין דברי הרמ"א מדוקדקין כ"כ שהרי אהא דסעיף ט' לא פליג רמ"א אם לא משום דהמחבר סתם וקאמר נפלים ושלא לטעות דדוקא הערלה אין מסירין קמ"ל דמי שהוא בחזקת נפל גם לקוברו אסור. ועוד י"ל דגם בספק נפל כההיא דסעיף ט' דעת רמ"א שמוטב להניח קבורתו עד אחר יו"ט כדי שיסיר ערלתו לפני הקבורה ולא קוברין ספק נפל אלא במת לאחר שמלו אותו או בנפל נקבה וכן כתבו איזה אחרונים. מיהו בתינוק שלא מלו אותו מחמת חולי וכה"ג ומת לאחר שלשים בודאי קוברין אותו ביו"ט ומסירין אז גם ערלתו. ודע דיש מן אחרונים שחולקין אעיקר דיני דנפלים ולדידהו קבורת נפלים נמי מצוה ואם כן אפשר שיש עכ"פ להתיר ביו"ט שני על ידי עכו"ם ועיין בחכמת אדם כלל ק"ע ס"ז:

{48} Nefalim, etc.: it appears that he is not speaking of definite nefalim, for those it is forbidden to bury on Yom Tov, and if so, independently it is not relevant to circumcise them, for they circumcise them upon their grave, as the Mechaber wrote in Yoreh Deah, siman 263, se'if 5; rather he refers to the nefalim of se'if 9, whom we treat, regarding burial, with the presumption of viable children, and we occupy ourselves with their burial on Yom Tov; and even so, to fulfill the custom to circumcise them one should not permit, for this is not among the needs of burial.
{49} And it is forbidden to bury him: according to what we explained of the Mechaber's words, the Rama's words are not so precise, for regarding that of se'if 9 the Rama does not dispute, unless because the Mechaber stated plainly "nefalim," and lest one err that specifically the orlah they do not remove, it teaches us that one who is in the presumption of a nefel is also forbidden to bury. And one may further say that even regarding a doubtful nefel such as that of se'if 9, the Rama's view is that it is better to leave his burial until after Yom Tov so that he remove his orlah before the burial; and they bury a doubtful nefel only after he has been circumcised, or a female nefel; and so wrote some Acharonim. However, regarding a child whom they did not circumcise because of illness and the like, and he died after thirty [days], certainly they bury him on Yom Tov and then also remove his orlah. And know that some Acharonim dispute the main laws of nefalim, and according to them burial of nefalim is also a mitzvah; and if so, it is possible that one should at least permit on the second day of Yom Tov through a non-Jew; and see Chochmas Adam, klal 170, se'if 7.
